_about: Registry for mind-arbiter. Copy to ~/.config/mind/models.json and edit.
Never put an API key here: name where it lives with key_env / key_env_file.
weight_gib is what the model needs resident, including KV and, for a streaming
model, its expert cache. The arbiter evicts others only until that much is free,
so an honest number here is what keeps a swap from OOMing the box.
First non-opt_in entry is the default when a request names no model.

_slots_note: slots is the server's slot count -- /props reports it as total_slots, and it
is NOT 1 by default: --parallel defaults to auto, which chose 4 here. The
arbiter saves and restores each slot by index, so a wrong number silently
leaves the extra slots cold. Set it to 0 to turn KV persistence off.
Requires llama-server to be started with --slot-save-path DIR; without that
Measured here with -c 131072: a 3926-token slot saved in 82 ms and the file
was ~330 MiB, of which ~190 MiB is context checkpoints rather than KV; the
marginal KV cost is ~20 KiB/token, so a full slot projects to ~2.5 GiB and
four to ~10 GiB. Files are overwritten on every save, so that is a ceiling,
not growth -- but put the directory somewhere with room for it.

_note: opt_in keeps it out of the default route: a cold start reads 70-123 GiB to
warm its expert cache, which no KV persistence can save. Points at the kyuz0
fork build because mainline ROCm prefill measured 0.90 t/s against the
fork's 22.05 t/s; see speed-bench/deepseek-v4.1-flash-gfx1151.md in ds4.
That fork build is missing two ROCm correctness fixes (f3ee00a, 5c3b0a4).
weight_gib 88 matches the 76GB expert cache above, not auto sizing, which
planned 100.97 GiB -- more than a sweep watchdog once killed on this box.
A dense 33.1B whose KV is 208 KiB/token at f16 (52 layers x 8 KV heads x 128),
about ten times MiniCPM's measured ~20 KiB. So the context, not the weights,
is what sizes it: Q4_K_M is 19.4 GiB, but the advertised 524288-token context
would want 104 GiB of KV and does not fit the pool at any cache type.
The unit runs -c 131072 with a q8_0 cache, measured at 34.1 GiB of the pool,
so weight_gib 36 leaves a small margin. Quantizing the cache is what makes
that context affordable: 65536 with an f16 cache measured 32.8 GiB, so this
is twice the context for 1.3 GiB. It costs 2% of prefill and some cache
numerics, and nothing else -- verified that it does not break persistence,
which would have ruled it out: a slot saved in 78 ms and restored into a
different slot index in 24 ms.
This is the first model on this box that need not evict another: resident
beside MiniCPM with 55.3 GiB still available.
Slot files measured 110.6 KiB/token (466 MB for 4113 tokens, against 877 MB
for the same prompt at f16), so a full pair projects to ~14 GiB. Round trip
on the deployed unit: 13967 ms of prefill came back as 106 ms, save 2/2 in
under a second, reload in 8 s.
Prefill is 285 tok/s on a 6329-token prompt and decode 9.7 tok/s. Decode is a
sixth of MiniCPM's 68.6 because it is dense -- every token reads all 19.4 GiB,
where MiniCPM activates ~3B of its 35B. Measure prefill with a large prompt:
43 tokens reports 109.6 tok/s, which is latency and not comparable to a
pp2048 figure. A sweep of -ub 512/1024/2048 gave 281/285/288 tok/s, so the
batch settings inherited from the MiniCPM unit make no difference here.
Decode reaches 37.9 tok/s on an edit-this-file prompt because the unit runs
--spec-type ngram-simple: 3.7x, with 249 of 249 drafted tokens accepted. That
is the only lever that matters here -- plain decode moves 202 GB/s of a ~256
GB/s pool, so no engine reading these weights one token at a time can be much
quicker, which is why the engine stays llama.cpp. The flag costs bit-exact
reproducibility on free prose; see the unit for the measurement.
opt_in because its benchmark claims are the vendor's own and unreplicated.
UNTESTED on this box. The 137 GiB file cannot be resident in a ~122 GiB
pool, so it streams; weight_gib is a guess until measured. Left out of the
live registry until someone runs it.
external means the arbiter never starts or stops it and never counts it
against local memory -- another host owns its lifecycle. Useful so one
endpoint can offer both local models and a remote host's.
